d166b8e4f7264b1e: SINGAPORE: The dollar was on shaky ground on Monday, despite a ramp-up in US rate hike bets as Middle East tensions raised the prospect of broader inflationary pressures that could force global central banks to tighten policy in tandem.
A shift in sentiment towards the Japanese yen and worries about ever-growing US debt and policy uncertainties also weighed on the greenback.

Moves in currencies were largely subdued in early Asia trade with US markets closed for a holiday, though the dollar struggled to sustain a brief lift it received from Friday's blowout US jobs report.
The euro was up marginally at US$1.1618, while sterling was little changed at US$1.3519. Against a basket of currencies, the dollar fell 0.07% to 99.09, not far from its recent low of 98.558.
Traders moved to price in a roughly 57% chance the Federal Reserve will hike rates this month in the wake of the nonfarm payrolls release, with much now depending on Friday's inflation data.

"A hot CPI print would all but seal a September hike and underpin a firmer US dollar. A cooler reading would strengthen the case for a hold and leave the US dollar vulnerable to a dovish Fed repricing," said Elias Haddad, global head of markets strategy at BBH.
"Even if a September Fed hike becomes a done deal, we doubt the US dollar will make new cyclical highs. Tightening by other major central banks limits policy divergence."

The inflationary impulse from still-elevated oil prices is a major reason the European Central Bank is seen certain to lift rates to 2.75% on Thursday. Futures also imply a 75% chance of another hike to 3.0% by December.
Likewise, markets are pricing a 75% chance the Bank of Japan (BOJ) will raise rates a quarter point at its meeting on Sept 18, with a 60% probability of another move by December.
The yen rose more than 0.2% to 155.88 per dollar on Monday, extending gains after Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi's economic adviser projected a BOJ hike this month.
The Japanese currency had surged more than 2% last week, following a confluence of factors including the unwinding of carry trades and expectations of capital repatriation that would boost the yen.

Eric Robertsen, global head of research and chief strategist at Standard Chartered, said that while carry trades have been among the strongest macro performers year-to-date despite a surge in borrowing costs globally, the "recent burst" of yen strength is a "potential threat to carry outperformance".
"If the JPY were to strengthen persistently, this may signal that the increase in JPY and USD rates is starting to trigger a change in asset allocation," he said.
In other currencies, the Australian dollar advanced 0.12% to US$0.7208, while the New Zealand dollar was flat at US$0.5880.
Bitcoin steadied above the US$80,000 level and was last at US$80,145.95, having drawn support recently as investors diversified away from the dollar into other assets.
9435472a33abd63d: JAKARTA, Sept 7 — Malaysian travellers flying from or transiting through Soekarno-Hatta International Airport (CGK) in Jakarta have been advised to regularly check their flight status following disruptions caused by volcanic ash from Mount Anak Krakatau.
The Malaysian Embassy in Jakarta said the volcanic ash had forced the temporary closure of several airports and disrupted international flights, including services to and from Kuala Lumpur.

“Malaysian visitors who have flights from or through CGK are advised to check their flight status with their respective airlines from time to time for information regarding flight rescheduling or alternative routes,” it said in an advisory on Monday.

In its latest update at midnight, Indonesia’s Transport Ministry said Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and six other airports would remain temporarily closed until 8.59am local time on Monday due to volcanic ash from Anak Krakatau.

The other airports are Radin Inten II in Lampung, Halim Perdanakusuma in Jakarta, Husein Sastranegara in Bandung, Budiarto in Tangerang, Pondok Cabe in South Tangerang and M. Taufik Kiemas in Lampung.
The embassy also advised Malaysian visitors to keep abreast of developments and comply with instructions from local authorities, particularly regarding the spread of volcanic ash.
For consular assistance, the embassy can be contacted at +62 21 522 4947 during office hours and +62 813 8081 3036 after office hours. — Bernama
782a8b952597bbeb: PETALING JAYA: The High Court in Johor Bahru has ordered a contractor to pay RM180,000 after finding that its construction works caused repeated flooding over 17 months at a surau and adjoining agricultural land in Johor.

Judicial commissioner Noradura Hamzah held Syarikat Pembinaan Yeoh Tiong Lay Sdn Bhd (YTL Construction) liable for negligence and private nuisance over the temporary culvert works at Sungai Sebulong, carried out as part of the Gemas–Johor Bahru Electrified Double-Track Project.
The court found that YTL Construction’s temporary drainage arrangement was inadequate and altered the natural flow of water, causing repeated flooding from November 2020 to April 2022.

The plaintiffs, Ghazali Ismail, chairman of the Economic and Development Committee for the Management Committee of Kariah Surau Ar Rahman, and Sharom Othman, public officer of Persatuan Komuniti Agro Tiong Larkin Jaya, claimed the flooding damaged the surau, religious items, furniture, crops and fish and prawn ponds.

YTL Construction denied liability, arguing that the area was naturally prone to flooding because of its low-lying terrain, heavy rainfall and rubbish in the river. It also said its construction works were approved by the relevant authorities.

However, Noradura found there was no major flooding at the surau before YTL Construction began its works. She said the flooding started after the temporary culverts were installed and stopped after a permanent culvert became operational on April 7, 2022.
She said YTL Construction's insurance adjuster’s report, evidence from the local authority and admissions by the contractor’s witnesses supported the plaintiffs’ case.

The judge also found that YTL Construction failed to properly design, inspect and maintain the temporary culvert, and left the permanent culvert unopened for more than 13 months after it was structurally completed.
Ghazali was awarded RM95,000 in special damages while Sharom received RM20,000.
The court also awarded RM40,000 in general damages for continuing nuisance and RM25,000 in aggravated damages, bringing total damages to RM180,000.
YTL Construction was ordered to pay 5% annual interest on the damages and RM120,000 in costs.

Noradura said aggravated damages were justified by YTL Construction's conduct, including concealing a stop-work order from its consultant engineer and withholding insurance adjuster’s reports from him.
Fairuz Abdullah and Ismail Tahir represented Ghazali and Sharom while Goh Toh Jen appeared for YTL Construction.
c3e6659cfefafc87: SYDNEY: Asian shares rallied on Monday as the robust US jobs report was seen as positive for global growth even as it narrowed the odds on a rise in interest rates, while oil edged higher after the US and Iran attacked ships in the Gulf.

Tehran said it will announce a restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz in coming days, after US forces hit three Iranian tankers and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships.
As a result, Brent added 0.2% to reach US$96.45 a barrel, having climbed almost 10% last week, while US crude rose 0.4% to $91.85 a barrel .

That inflationary impulse raises the stakes for a key reading of US consumer prices this week, and is a major reason the European Central Bank is seen as certain to lift rates to 2.75% on Thursday. Futures also imply a 75% chance of another hike to 3.0% by December.
The risk of hawkish guidance from the ECB after the rate hike kept European stocks on edge on Monday. EUROSTOXX 50 futures and DAX futures eased 0.1%, while FTSE futures were flat.
On Wall Street, a US holiday kept turnover light with both S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures a fraction lower.
A key focus this week is the US August CPI report on Friday where median forecasts are for a rise of 0.2% in the core, with a risk of 0.3%.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei rebounded 2.0%, after losing a similar amount last week, while South Korea rallied 3.0%. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan added 0.9%.

Rising bond yields remain a drag for equity valuations, with Treasury 10-year yields near their highest since late 2023 at 4.7840%. A high CPI reading would likely see yields edge closer to the psychological 5.0% barrier.
For the Federal Reserve, last week's upbeat payrolls report has left markets pricing a 58% chance of a hike when it meets on September 16, and 70% for a move in October.
Bruce Kasman, global head of economics at JPMorgan, is looking for core CPI to rise 0.21% which he thinks would be low enough to keep the Fed on hold, if only for now.
Likewise, markets are pricing a 75% chance the Bank of Japan will raise rates a quarter point at its meeting on Sept 18, with a 60% probability of another move by December.
"Central bank patience through the energy shock has been supportive of asset prices and the credit cycle," said Kasman. "However, central banks are now on the move."

"We forecast two more hikes from the ECB and BoJ before year-end," he added. "There is also a strong case for the Fed to move earlier and more aggressively than our baseline forecast for a December hike."

In currency markets, the dollar index got only a mild lift from the jobs report as worries about ever-growing US debt and policy uncertainties erode the purchasing power of the currency, driving investors to scarce assets including gold.
The dollar index stood at 99.135, not far from recent lows at 98.558. The euro held at US$1.1614, within sight of the August top at US$1.1711.
The dollar was a tick easier at 156.07 yen, and still threatening major support at 155.00 after losing 2.4% last week as the yen rallied on speculation about a more aggressive BoJ tightening.
In commodities, gold was steady at US$4,426 an ounce, after finding support at US$4,282 last week.
b7dc9778a278d85b: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 7 — The Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) has opened an investigation into delays in the distribution of supplementary compound fertiliser to padi farmers in Kedah.

In a statement today, MACC said its Kedah branch opened the investigation following a complaint lodged by the Pertubuhan Persaudaraan Pesawah Malaysia (Pesawah) organisation on Aug 26 over delays in the supply of the fertiliser.

The supplier appointed by the Agriculture and Food Security Ministry (known by its Malay initials KPKM) has delayed the fertiliser needed by padi farmers in the 100,000-hectare area under the Muda Agricultural Development Authority (Mada).
“Kedah MACC is conducting the investigation to look into not only the criminal aspect, but also any governance weaknesses that may have contributed to the delay,” the statement read.
MACC said it had so far recorded the statement of a witness from Pesawah and received several relevant documents.
“MACC welcomes the call and concern expressed by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim over the issue and has engaged with KPKM and Mada for further investigation,” the statement said.
Meanwhile, MACC chief commissioner Datuk Seri Abd Halim Aman, when contacted, confirmed the matter and said the investigation was opened under Section 18 of the MACC Act 2009.

The media had previously reported a call by Pengkalan Kundor assemblyman Mardhiyyah Johari for the government to consider compensation for padi farmers who suffered losses due to delays in the distribution of supplementary compound fertiliser, or ‘Baja Padi 3’, in the Mada area.
The delay has affected about 38,000 farmers, involving 78,117 hectares of padi fields.
On Aug 18, Mada said 22 per cent, or 137,560 bags, of Baja Padi 3 had been supplied against the total requirement of 616,015 bags. — Bernama
44454864c14c6e40: NEW DELHI, Sept 7 — A building collapse in the Indian capital New Delhi killed at least three people yesterday, local media reports said, as authorities worked to rescue those trapped in the rubble.

The building, housing mostly students, came crashing down about midday in the south-western Satya Niketan area of the city, with police and disaster response personnel cautiously lifting the rubble using heavy machinery.
Three people died in the accident, according to The Hindu newspaper and other local media reports, quoting unnamed fire services officials.
Nine people were rescued from under the rubble, with five of them taken to a hospital in critical condition, the reports said.
The exact number of people feared trapped was not immediately known.
An adjacent building has been vacated over fears it could also collapse.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the incident was “distressing” and offered “condolences to those who lost their loved ones”, according to a statement from his office.
TV images showed rescuers pulling a young man out from the rubble and another trapped under a block of fallen concrete slab, with only his face visible.
Delhi’s Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said she was “deeply concerned” by the incident.
“Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped and provide immediate assistance to the affected families,” Gupta said in a social media post.
The Satya Niketan area is home to hundreds of university students living in crowded, privately-owned accommodations as paying guests.
Building collapses are frequent in India, and illegal structures — often home to migrant workers and students — are common in big cities.
Last year, at least 11 people were killed after a residential building collapsed in the northeastern district of the capital city. — AFP
459cb9b92b838718: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 7 — The ringgit opened slightly higher against the US dollar today, buoyed by expectations of a potential United States (US) interest rate hike following stronger-than-expected US non-farm payrolls (NFP) data.
At 8 am, the local currency inched up to 4.0415/0500 against the greenback from last Friday’s close of 4.0425/0465.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the higher-than-expected NFP suggests the US Federal Reserve (Fed) is likely to raise its benchmark interest rate at the upcoming Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Sept 15-16.
“The NFP came in at 162,000 in August, well above the consensus forecast of 55,000, while July’s figure was revised up to 21,000 from the initial estimate of 23,000.
“Labour force participation rate improved to 61.6 per cent after experiencing a persistent drop since January this year,” he told Bernama.
Mohd Afzanizam said Asian currencies may face a choppy trading session today, with the ringgit trading in a wider margin, potentially around 4.04 to 4.06 against the greenback.

1759f0a2fe51591b: SEPTEMBER 7 — Imagine spending months, perhaps even years, testing an idea. The experiment is carefully designed, samples are collected, and the data are painstakingly analysed. Expectations are understandably high. Perhaps the study will identify a promising new treatment, uncover a risk factor for disease, or confirm a relationship that scientists have long suspected.

Then the results come in. There is no significant difference. The treatment does not perform better than expected. The relationship you thought would appear in the data simply is not there. Has the research failed?
Not necessarily. In fact, such a result may be one of the most useful pieces of information that the research produces.

Scientific research usually begins with a question. Is drug A more effective than the existing treatment? Does a particular factor increase the risk of developing a disease? Are two biological processes related? When a well-designed study does not find sufficient evidence to support the original hypothesis, the outcome may be described as a negative or null result. Unfortunately, the word "negative" is easily mistaken for "failure". Scientifically, however, these are very different things.

Part of the problem is that we are naturally drawn to stories of scientific success. A new drug treats a previously difficult disease, scientists develop a technology that could save lives, or researchers discover a biological mechanism that helps explain a longstanding medical mystery. These findings are exciting, and understandably so. They attract public attention and make compelling headlines. Within academia, statistically significant or apparently novel findings have also historically been easier to publish than studies reporting that an expected effect was not found.

This creates what researchers call publication bias. Related to it is the "file drawer problem", where studies producing inconclusive, negative or null findings remain unpublished and effectively disappear from the scientific record. The consequences may be more serious than simply leaving some research unread.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Test tubes are seen in this undated illustrative picture. — Unsplash pic

Imagine that ten research groups independently test the same compound. Nine find no meaningful effect, but their findings are never published. One group reports a positive result, and that study appears in a journal. Anyone reading the published literature would see only that one positive result. The compound might therefore appear far more promising than the total body of evidence actually suggests.

This is why null results matter. Science depends not only on what we discover, but also on having as complete a picture of the evidence as possible. Knowing that an approach did not produce the expected result can itself help determine where research should go next.

It can also save considerable time, money and resources. If one laboratory reports through a rigorous study that a particular compound does not produce the expected effect, other researchers can take that evidence into account before investing resources in pursuing the same path. This is especially important when research is supported by public funds. Every ringgit spent repeating an avoidable dead end is a ringgit that could potentially have been used to investigate another promising question.

The stakes can be even higher in medical research. Finding that a treatment does not provide the expected benefit is important information. So is discovering that it performs no better than an existing treatment, or that its side effects outweigh its potential benefits. Such findings can help researchers and clinicians decide which approaches deserve further investigation and which assumptions need to be reconsidered. Knowing what does not work, in other words, helps narrow the search for what might.

Sometimes, however, an unexpected result does more than close one avenue of investigation. It opens another. Science does not progress only through experiments that confirm what researchers hoped to find. Some of its most interesting questions emerge precisely when the data refuse to cooperate with expectations.

Why did the expected relationship not appear? Was the original assumption incomplete? Is another factor influencing the outcome? Could the underlying biological mechanism be more complicated than previously thought? Questions like these can lead to new hypotheses and entirely different directions of research.

This is also why we should be careful about what we call a failed experiment. A genuinely poor experiment may fail because its design is flawed, its methods are inappropriate, its sample is inadequate, or its data are unreliable. That is very different from a rigorous experiment producing a result that happens not to support the original hypothesis. The more useful questions are whether the research question was sound, whether the study was properly designed, whether appropriate methods were used, and whether the data were analysed and reported transparently. If those standards are met, an unexpected answer is still an answer.

The scientific community has become increasingly aware of the problems created when positive findings receive disproportionate attention. One response has been greater emphasis on practices such as preregistration, where researchers specify their hypotheses, methods and analysis plans before examining the results. Such practices can improve transparency and reduce the temptation, whether conscious or otherwise, to adjust analyses after the fact simply to produce a more interesting or statistically significant finding.

But improving research practice is only part of the solution. Publication culture also has a role to play. The value of research should not depend solely on whether its findings can be labelled "positive" or "negative". The quality of the research question, the strength of the study design, methodological rigour, transparency and reliability of the evidence are ultimately more important.

The public, too, may benefit from a better understanding of how science actually progresses. Scientific discovery rarely follows a straight line from question to breakthrough. Behind one successful medicine may be dozens of compounds that did not work. Behind an accepted scientific explanation may be hundreds of experiments that challenged earlier assumptions and forced researchers to refine their understanding. Those apparently unremarkable findings are not separate from scientific progress. They are part of it.

Perhaps, then, we should be more careful with the word "failure" in research. A well-conducted experiment that does not find the expected relationship or effect is not necessarily wasted effort. It adds another piece to our collective understanding, sometimes by showing us where not to look and sometimes by forcing us to ask a better question.

A scientist's contribution is not always to prove that something is true. Sometimes it is to demonstrate, carefully and convincingly, that something we expected to happen does not. In science, discovering that we have taken the wrong path can be an important step towards finding the right one.
* Dr Manorenjitha Malar Sivanathan is a research officer at Pusat Kanser Tun Abdullah Ahmad Badawi (PKTAAB), Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM).

12685433eb72b004: PETALING JAYA: Kerjasama rasmi antara Umno dan PAS kini mempunyai peluang lebih baik untuk bertahan setelah ia tidak lagi dibayangi Bersatu, kata seorang penganalisis, yang menyokong gesaan agar kedua-dua parti itu menjadikan kerjasama itu sebagai rasmi.

Mazlan Ali dari Universiti Teknologi Malaysia memberitahu FMT bahawa perjanjian rasmi yang mengikat kepentingan kedua-dua parti akan memberikan lebih kestabilan berbanding sekadar persefahaman bersama.
Beliau berkata PAS dan Umno sebelum ini pernah bekerjasama dalam gabungan Muafakat Nasional (MN), tetapi pakatan itu akhirnya gagal kerana Umno tidak berpuas hati dengan hubungan PAS bersama Bersatu.

Bagaimanapun, katanya, landskap politik telah berubah sejak itu, dengan PAS memutuskan hubungan dengan Bersatu pada Jun lalu walaupun kedua-dua parti itu kekal sebagai rakan dalam Perikatan Nasional (PN).
Mazlan berkata pakatan tidak rasmi antara kedua-dua parti dalam PRN Johor dan Negeri Sembilan bukan jaminan bahawa kerjasama itu akan bertahan sehingga PRU akan datang.
“Hanya perjanjian rasmi membolehkan hubungan politik yang berkekalan antara kedua-dua parti,” katanya.
Menurutnya, sebarang perjanjian baharu mesti memperincikan dengan jelas perkara berkaitan pembahagian kerusi, kesetiaan antara parti dan pendirian bersama mengenai isu politik.
Bagaimanapun, isu yang boleh mencetuskan pertikaian ialah menentukan siapa yang akan mengetuai kerajaan sekiranya gabungan itu memenangi PRU akan datang.
“Pada masa ini, saya tidak pasti parti mana yang sanggup melepaskan jawatan perdana menteri kepada rakan kongsinya,” katanya.
Beliau menambah bahawa perbezaan yang ketara dan kekurangan kepercayaan masih wujud antara kedua-dua parti itu walaupun terdapat momentum yang jelas untuk memperbaharui kerjasama.

“Saya fikir idea MN, walaupun mudah disebut, tidak mudah direalisasikan. Masih terdapat banyak perbezaan antara kedua-dua parti (PAS dan Umno), dan tahap kepercayaan antara mereka masih rendah,” katanya.
Syaza Shukri dari Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia berkata piagam rasmi boleh memberikan kekuatan politik kepada kerjasama tidak rasmi dengan menjadikannya komitmen yang khusus.

Beliau berkata piagam itu boleh meyakinkan anggota parti bahawa kerjasama tersebut mendapat sokongan kedua-dua kepimpinan, memberikan kerangka kepada pemimpin negeri untuk berunding dan memberi isyarat kepada pengundi bahawa PAS dan Umno berhasrat mengelakkan pertandingan tiga penjuru.

Bagaimanapun, kepentingannya bergantung pada kandungannya. Pengisytiharan yang hanya berpusat pada perpaduan Melayu-Islam, tanpa aturan yang mengikat, akan kekal sebahagian besarnya sebagai simbolik, katanya.
Syaza berkata perjanjian baharu hanya akan berbeza daripada MN sekiranya kedua-dua parti menangani keadaan politik dan kekaburan yang menyumbang kepada keruntuhan pakatan terdahulu.

“Kedua-dua parti mesti bersetuju sama ada kerjasama mereka bersifat eksklusif, bagaimana hubungannya dengan BN, PN dan Pakatan Harapan (PH), serta parti mana yang ada keutamaan di kawasan yang dipertandingkan. Jika tidak, ia akan mengulangi kekaburan dalam MN dengan nama baharu,” katanya.

Beliau berkata kerjasama tidak rasmi menawarkan fleksibiliti tetapi terdedah kepada kenyataan yang bercanggah dan sabotaj oleh pemimpin parti, manakala perjanjian rasmi boleh menyediakan struktur yang diberi kuasa.
Bagaimanapun, menurut Syaza, rundingan tidak rasmi mungkin masih lebih realistik pada peringkat ini.

Sebarang piagam baharu, katanya, harus mentakrifkan kedudukan rakan politik sedia ada, menetapkan prinsip telus bagi pembahagian kerusi, mewujudkan mekanisme membuat keputusan bersama dan penyelesaian pertikaian, serta menyediakan peraturan mengenai disiplin parti dan komunikasi awam.
Piagam itu juga harus menjelaskan aturan selepas pilihan raya, termasuk sama ada mana-mana parti boleh berunding dengan gabungan ketiga dan bagaimana jawatan dalam kerajaan akan diagihkan.
d8a64695f0161dcf: NEW YORK: Data centres are running into a wall of public anger in the United States over their thirst for water and power.
The tech giants spending billions of dollars on them say the water part, at least, is solvable.
Data centres are the warehouses full of computer servers that run the internet and increasingly artificial intelligence.
The computers get hot, and keeping them cool takes water.

American chip giant Nvidia said in a June report that it can eliminate water consumption almost entirely at some facilities when deploying DSX, its newest system for designing and managing AI data centres.
It's a bold claim, and one the industry is under mounting pressure to make good on.
In 2025, data centres consumed 222 billion litres (59 billion gallons) of water worldwide for cooling, according to consultancy Rystad Energy.
Without adaptive measures, the figure could nearly triple to 644 billion litres by 2030, Rystad estimates. Steps to limit the growth could keep it under double.
Nvidia's new method uses a closed-loop cooling system in which liquid flows directly through the servers, as close as possible to the chips, whose temperature can rise above 80°C (176°F).

The problem is that "there's a pretty direct trade-off between how much water is used and how much energy is used" for temperature control, said Andy Masley, an independent researcher who covers AI and data centres.
Cutting back on water use usually means more power, as the liquid in those sealed pipes still has to be cooled down somehow, usually by blowing air over it – and that takes electricity.
Nvidia gets around some of this by letting the liquid enter the servers warmer than usual, at 45°C.
Most other closed-loop systems ran at about 32°C in 2024, according to the Uptime Institute, which certifies data centres.
By starting with warmer water, Nvidia does not need to pump in cooled air year-round.
"Simple fans circulating the air" are often enough, though sometimes a mix of methods is needed, said Josh Parker, Nvidia's head of sustainability.
At sites in extreme climates, or during a heat wave, chill airflow or water evaporation is still necessary.
Public relations
Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Meta told AFP that they also use closed-loop systems, which they said involve no net water loss.

The two cloud computing giants, which have been expanding their already huge data centre footprints, used more water overall between 2022 and 2025, but their water use efficiency improved by 25% at Microsoft and 37% at AWS, according to their most recent sustainability reports.
There is no industry-wide consistency, however, in how companies report data on so-called environmental, social and governance (ESG) efforts.
Elon Musk's SpaceX, now a major player in data centres after it acquired its artificial intelligence company xAI, has never published an ESG report.
In June, ratings agency MSCI gave SpaceX its lowest ESG score.

"Because water is generally much cheaper than electricity," companies have less incentive to cut water use on cost grounds alone, said Shaolei Ren, an engineering professor at the University of California, Riverside.
"There are incentives," Ren said, but they have more to do with public relations amid the growing backlash to data centres across the US.
Another obstacle is that upgrading an older data centre to newer, less thirsty technology is expensive.
That may matter less than it sounds.

Older data centres are smaller and less powerful than the enormous new ones being built now, so they need less cooling in the first place, said Minh K. Le, who leads data centre and hydrogen research at Rystad.
And the water a data centre uses directly is only part of the story.
Water is used to generate the electricity that powers the data centre and to manufacture its chips and servers.
In the United States, that hidden water use can be twice the amount a data centre consumes on its own.

8d713e003d1cb1bf: From Moaz Nair

Formal Umno-PAS political relations go back to the time the Islamic party was integrated with Barisan Nasional in 1973. However, this collaboration culminated in friction, which subsequently led to the declaration of a state of emergency in Kelantan in 1977.

Four decades later, in the wake of the 2018 general election, the two parties formalised a renewed alliance, known as Muafakat Nasional which eventually reached an impasse when PAS elected to form Perikatan Nasional alongside Bersatu, a strategic manoeuvre that encountered vehement opposition from Umno.

Despite top-tier leadership efforts to push for a MN 2.0 or initiate partnerships under the "Rumah Bangsa" initiative, grassroots factions and leaders from both echelons concede that such reunification lacks sustainability if it remains merely seasonal and transactional for electoral gains.
History has shown that there are no guarantees that an alliance between Umno and PAS would not eventually fall apart.

History has also shown that, although Umno and PAS may draw from the same Malay-Muslim voter base, their relationship has often shifted. They have alternated between working together and confronting each other, depending on changing power dynamics and political survival.
Although “ummah unity” is often invoked to promote political stability, several structural issues could still reignite discord between the two parties.
Demographic and geographic overlap

The two parties have historically engaged in zero-sum competition within the same voter enclaves, specifically rural, Malay-majority constituencies. Consequently, the delineation of parliamentary and state assembly seats regularly precipitates hierarchical friction.
Deadlocks routinely emerge when determining incumbency or candidacy rights in areas designated as "winnable seats", a phenomenon previously observed during initialisation of the MN framework.
Power and leadership hegemony
Establishing the supreme leadership hierarchy, particularly concerning the premiership, remains a highly contentious point of friction.
Should PAS secure a larger parliamentary bloc than Umno, questions over who should lead the alliance could trigger intense internal power struggles and destabilise the partnership.
The trust deficit

Based on past political developments, Umno leaders remain cautious and sceptical of PAS's calls for unity. Sentiments regarding a "breach of trust" are frequently resurrected due to PAS's strategic pivot toward Bersatu within Perikatan Nasional.
This multi-alignment strategy, defined by a propensity to switch partners to secure political survival, directly exacerbates deep-seated institutional mistrust between the two parties.
Ideological divergence
Umno has traditionally leaned toward technocracy, economic development, and state-centric pragmatic policies.
Its political approach is ostensibly secular-nationalist and inclusive, as evidenced by its long-standing history of inter-ethnic cooperation with the MCA and MIC since pre-independence days.

Conversely, PAS prioritises Islamism as its foundational ideology, relying on an electoral doctrine rooted predominantly in a single ethnic demographic. This ideological divergence frequently engenders socio-political polemics during the formulation of public policy.
Strategic dilemma

Umno loyalists and political analysts currently face a strategic dilemma regarding proposed alliances with PAS. Umno's political hegemony since independence has relied substantially on its capacity to capture non-Malay swing votes, particularly in straight-fight scenarios against PAS.
Closer alignment with PAS risks alienating non-Malay voters, a trajectory exemplified by the electoral marginalisation of Gerakan after integrating into PN.

Furthermore, realistic anxieties persist that Umno risks being integrated or subverted by PAS, given that PAS currently commands a superior grassroots machinery and a significantly larger parliamentary presence.

This structural reality threatens to relegate Umno to "junior partner" status, exposing the party to gradual marginalisation compared to the relatively egalitarian power balance they maintained in 2019.
Politics is about pragmatism, meaning no alliance or rivalry lasts forever.
While Umno and PAS possess the capacity to forge new alignments based on the shared imperative of countering a common political enemy, their capacity to sustain such cooperation remains fragile.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

0003a86f9740b0fb: Malaysians recently enjoyed a public holiday on our National Day. Many also enjoyed the week-long school holidays while some got a hattrick of celebrations – an extra day for Selangor residents for the state topping the medals table at the recent Sukma inter-state games.
It’s a pretty good deal for many, including state politicians who got to give out the good news to Selangor’s residents at no cost to themselves because it’s the employers who foot the bill.

As a retiree I didn’t get to enjoy an extra day's holiday nor did I get holiday pay for working on the day. But at least I’m not an employer who has to foot the extra costs or deal with the disruptions caused by it.

Declaring a casual public holiday is a misguided attempt to buy goodwill from the rakyat. Either elections must be around the corner, or it’s become a reflex action for an ad hoc public holiday to be created.

The economy doesn’t benefit from this: costs go up and benefits are reduced to society at large. But you cannot argue about giving workers additional respite from their days at the office or factories. We have laws that require us to observe public holidays, of which we have a lot, scheduled and ad hoc, plus personal paid vacations, with most companies providing more than what is stipulated.

I guess if somebody very important passes away, or we achieve something truly epic – we win the World Cup! – then perhaps a public holiday is deserving. But lets examine the reason public holidays are declared in the first place.

They are meant to allow us to observe such holidays appropriately – perhaps by celebrating, marching in the street, holding celebrations, visiting families and friends or fulfilling cultural or religious obligations.

If you stay at home and don’t celebrate the event, then why are you deserving of a paid day off? I can tell you if Malaysia wins the World Cup I’ll be running myself ragged for perhaps days in an orgy of celebrations, and I certainly would welcome the public holiday.

But I remember a state declared an ad hoc holiday in three consecutive years purely because it made it to the final of the Malaysia Cup football competition. Not won it, just made it to the final, which it managed to lose each time.

I remember the business disruptions, and especially the withering looks from my foreign bosses and colleagues signalling – what kind of rubbish is this? I had no good answer then, and certainly none now either.

Disruptions didn’t just happen to businesses; they happen to normal people too. Most government and business services are closed with hardly any notice. Think about the disruptions to our everyday life in our dealings with the courts or passport offices or many other government as well as commercial services.
Feeling entitled

But the biggest problem is this: the state or national leaders also know we gain nothing from these public holidays. People are not grateful just for an extra day off. They won't work harder when they get back to their workplace, and neither would they change their voting preferences.

We do it because somehow we as the rakyat feel entitled to such perks, and the leaders who declare these holidays feel they are expected to do it, or else they’d be judged negatively if they didn’t oblige with this “generosity”.

Entitlement is becoming a huge problem in Malaysia. We have many things started by the government in good faith, whether affirmative action programmes or economic subsidies for some of the costs of living. Over time, however, these “privileges” have become “rights”, even if none of them have ever been voted in parliament into laws and statues.

When you feel entitled, you feel any questions on your entitlements are wrong or disrespectful or political, or all of them. Logic and justifications go out of the window, and emotions and outrage come into play. This being Malaysia, race and religion often get into the noise and make everything complicated and nasty.

I doubt if the political leaders debate the merits or otherwise on such ad hoc holidays. Most are smart enough to know that the negative impacts outweigh the positive, but somehow feel they’re under pressure to give the rakyat their “entitlement”.

In the end it’s a lose-lose for everybody. Many rakyat get something they haven’t earned, which just motivates them to expect even more unearned goodies. The economic drivers have to absorb the disruptions, and of course pass the negative impacts of higher costs or lower profits back to the population.

We may probably have gone too far down the road for any brave political leaders to say enough with this nonsense. That’s a shame, because we certainly don’t need to add to our growing lists of entitlements. We have more than enough already.

5122b4c7a7f37db0: In the last five years, six youth-led, anti-establishment uprisings have fundamentally reshaped South Asia’s political landscape.

The movements had much in common: they all reflected young people’s aspirations, digital savvy, economic frustrations, and disillusionment with governing elites. But the political systems in which they unfolded process grievances in vastly different ways, leading to sharply divergent outcomes.

The story begins in Myanmar, where the military’s February 2021 overthrow of a democratically elected government triggered popular protests. Unconstrained by concerns about democratic legitimacy, the new regime launched a violent crackdown.

With the peaceful restoration of democracy off the table, a generation of young people had little choice but to form civilian defense forces alongside armed ethnically based organisations. The result was a grinding civil war.

Sri Lanka’s March 2022 Aragalaya movement arose from economic collapse. Dry fuel pumps, prolonged power cuts, and sovereign insolvency destroyed the legitimacy of the Rajapaksa dynasty, which had ruled for the better part of two decades. Protests roiled the island, with demonstrators eventually occupying the presidential palace.

Yet, unlike Myanmar, Sri Lanka did not face surging violence, let alone a prolonged armed conflict. Instead, president Gotabaya Rajapaksa submitted to popular pressure and resigned within the constitutional framework.

In Pakistan, riots erupted in May 2023, following the arrest of former prime minister Imran Khan. This was a case of a populist movement mobilising behind a charismatic leader to challenge the military’s dominance—and it was met with a troop deployment, an internet shutdown, and the dismantling of the opposition’s formal party structures. The “hybrid” regime was preserved, at the cost of persistent political alienation.
Bangladesh’s July 2024 uprising demonstrated how a narrow policy dispute—in this case, student opposition to a skewed quota system for civil-service jobs—can turn into a revolution.
As protests against prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s autocratic regime escalated, Hasina deployed troops to enforce a curfew—with an order to shoot violators on sight.
When the military ultimately refused, Hasina’s hold on power collapsed. She fled the country, opening the way for an interim government to take over.

In Nepal, the September 2025 protests targeted not a single leader, but an oligarchic political class, which had been playing a decade-long game of prime ministerial “musical chairs” while most Nepali youths struggled with soaring unemployment and a lack of opportunity.
For a frustrated Gen Z, a government ban on major social-media platforms was the last straw: using VPNs and alternative apps, Nepal’s youth organised a massive protest.

The authorities attempted to crush it by force, but the protesters fought back, driving the elites out without destroying the parliamentary framework. Nepalis went on to elect a 35-year-old prime minister.
Finally, this summer, India experienced widespread student-led protests, sparked by leaks of university entrance examinations and fuelled by growing anxiety over jobless growth.

Far from threatening the constitutional order, however, the movement confirmed that order’s resilience, as the government offered critical concessions, accepting the education minister’s resignation and proposing administrative and policy reforms with a view towards redirecting protest energy back through established democratic channels.

These six cases show that hyper-connectivity and economic and political alienation are a potent combination. The first fully digitally native generation, Gen Z uses platforms like TikTok, WhatsApp, and Discord to bypass entrenched party structures and orchestrate mass mobilisations.
But that is not all that stands out about Gen Z’s protest style. Unlike their predecessors, today’s protesters are motivated by a sense that they have nothing to lose.

It is not hard to see why: with their economic prospects drastically diminished, despite high educational attainment, what today’s young people see are not flawed institutions in need of reform, but a predatory system robbing them of a viable future.

This imbues their protests with a visceral, existential urgency and makes them resistant to state co-optation. Unimpressed by incremental concessions, they are willing to confront institutional repression head-on.

For all they have in common, these six cases also underscore the difference institutional structures make. In closed regimes that treat power as non-negotiable, such as Myanmar and Pakistan, popular discontent inevitably results in political fragmentation or chronic instability.

In rigid civilian autocracies like Hasina’s Bangladesh, protest is either repressed or revolutionary: the system is unmovable until a single crack—such as the military refusing an order—brings down the whole edifice.
Conversely, systems that allow for political transitions or administrative conciliation can survive generational shocks.

Sri Lanka achieved a peaceful electoral realignment, and Nepal engineered a political reset, which created space for “outsider” political forces. India, for its part, showed how a robust multiparty democracy accommodates discontent before it metastasizes into systemic crisis.

These episodes hold several important lessons. For starters, celebrating aggregate macroeconomic growth but ignoring youth unemployment and systemic corruption is a recipe for instability. Younger generations view economic opportunity as inseparable from political accountability—and they will, sooner or later, demand both.

Moreover, military-dominated governance is poorly suited for this era of hyper-connectivity. While crackdowns and coercion can suppress dissent temporarily, they destroy state legitimacy over time. Relying on them risks prolonged civil disorder.

Finally, dismantling systemic corruption is only the first step. Durable institutions, with democratic pressure valves and credible mechanisms for addressing young people’s aspirations, are also essential.
That is why India’s recent uprising reaffirmed its democracy, while Nepal and Sri Lanka, as well as Bangladesh, have faced considerable post-uprising instability.

The Arab Spring revolutions a decade and a half ago ultimately ended in military counter-revolution, autocratic revival, or institutional paralysis, owing to absent or fragile democratic legacies and ideological hijacking. But many South Asian societies possess deep parliamentary traditions, vibrant civil societies, and functional constitutional mechanisms.

If South Asian countries can harness young people’s activist energy to deliver effective, responsive governance and job-creating reforms, they will put themselves on a path towards a brighter, more resilient, and more prosperous future. And they will become a model for how the Global South can align demographic weight with democratic accountability.

Shashi Tharoor, a former UN under-secretary-general and former Indian minister of state for external affairs and minister of state for human resource development, is a fourth-term elected member of Parliament for the opposition Indian National Congress.

40dc1ce96b111174: The prospect of a negative leap second – combined with decades of irritation over leap seconds generally – looks set to inspire a bit of global procrastination among international timekeepers. Next month, the General Conference on Weights and Measures is set to vote on effectively calling time on leap seconds. A draft resolution [PDF] would make Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) continuous from May 20, 2027, and allow the difference between UTC and UT1, a measure of time based on Earth's rotation, to reach as much as one hour. Leap seconds keep UTC, which is based on atomic clocks, within 0.9 seconds of time determined by the slightly wobbly rotation of our home planet. Since the system was introduced in 1972, 27 leap seconds have been added to UTC. The urgency comes partly from a slight increase in Earth's rotational speed in recent years, raising the possibility of an adjustment never attempted before: a negative leap second. Experts convened by international timekeeping bodies estimated a 30 percent probability that one would be needed by 2035. Many computer systems were designed on the assumption that a leap second would always be added rather than removed, explained Setnam Shemar, principal scientist at the UK's National Physical Laboratory (NPL). "Most digital architectures and network time servers are hardcoded under the assumption that leap seconds are strictly additive. Losing a second could trigger severe disruption across critical national infrastructure, including telecommunications, electricity grids, and satellite navigation systems," he said. The risks posed by a negative leap second – and leap seconds generally – are behind the proposal to let UTC diverge from rotational time by as much as an hour, which is due to be put to a vote in October. Shemar said the proposal would remove the need for further leap-second adjustments for many years. "This would remove the risks entirely for a very long time. Next month's resolution is likely to pass since it will be based on the outcome of a majority vote of the national delegates from many different countries, and most of them have been keen to end leap seconds for several years due to the risks posed to national infrastructure." UTC would be unlikely to diverge from rotational time by a full hour for at least a thousand years, Shemar said. If humankind lasts that long, it might be the least of our worries. ®

a4b3f6287a5a5dbc: Saya mengikuti muktamar PAS yang sedang berlangsung di Pengkalan Chepa, Kelantan dari jauh. Ramai yang hadir dan ramai juga wakil yang berpidato dan dari situ, banyak persoalan yang timbul di benak saya.
Saya tidak banyak mendengar ucapan khusus tentang masalah negeri atau negara, apalagi tentang hal-hal yang berkait dengan ekonomi rakyat atau ekonomi negara.

Ataupun tentang hutang negara yang begitu tinggi, masalah kewangan defisit, perbelanjaan kerajaan berlebihan, Belanjawan 2027, pembahagian hasil dan pendapatan, serta bagaimana semua ini akan diuruskan sekiranya PAS mengambil alih tampuk pemerintahan negara.

Persoalan saya di sini, bukan sekadar sama ada PAS mampu memenangi pilihan raya akan datang dan membentuk kerajaan. Mereka yang hadir nampaknya percaya dan agak yakin. Sebagai contoh, 'Time for PAS to lead with its own PM candidate, says youth leader', satu impian besar yang perlu sedikit kajian dan penjelasan.
Persoalan yang lebih besar ialah: adakah PAS benar-benar mempunyai keupayaan, kepakaran dan kerangka dasar yang jelas untuk mentadbir sebuah negara majmuk?

Berapa ramai pakar ekonomi, tokoh fiskal atau kewangan, perdagangan, pendidikan, industri, pengangkutan dan pembangunan dalam PAS? Apakah mereka sekadar bergantung harap kepada rakan politiknya semata-mata?

Siapa dalam kalangan mereka yang berkaliber untuk membentuk dasar baharu? Siapakah antara yang hadir, mampu melakukan perubahan pengurusan negara supaya Malaysia bukan sekadar ditadbir, tetapi benar-benar dimajukan ke tahap yang lebih baik dan lebih tinggi?
Memerintah Malaysia bukan hanya sekadar menjadi perdana menteri, menteri atau timbalan menteri.

Ia memerlukan satu pasukan yang mempunyai kepakaran, pengalaman dan keberanian untuk membuat keputusan yang sukar, khususnya apabila berhadapan dengan masalah fiskal, hutang negara, subsidi, pelaburan, perdagangan, pendidikan, hubungan antarabangsa dan hubungan antara kerajaan persekutuan dengan Sabah dan Sarawak.
Rakyat perlu tahu apakah sebenarnya visi dan misi PAS untuk Malaysia.
Dasar fiskal
Pada pandangan saya, antara perkara paling penting yang akan menentukan kejayaan atau kegagalan mana-mana kerajaan baharu ialah dasar fiskal mereka.

Dasar fiskal ini menentukan bagaimana kerajaan memperolehi hasil, siapa yang membayar cukai, bagaimana wang dibelanjakan, siapa yang menerima bantuan dan bagaimana defisit serta hutang negara dikawal, menjadi seimbang atau ada lebihan (surplus). Di sinilah PAS perlu memberikan perhatian utama dengan pandangan yang pandai, padat dan serius.

Cadangan “Please change the movie on tax” oleh Geoffrey Williams, misalnya, merupakan satu cadangan dasar fiskal yang menarik dan wajar diberi perhatian. Tiada seorang pun yang hadir di muktamar PAS menyentuh tentang hal yang penting seperti ini.
Cadangan menggunakan electronic payment tax (EPT) sebagai mekanisme percukaian baharu, jika dilaksanakan dengan reka bentuk yang betul, berpotensi mengubah cara kerajaan mengutip hasil.

Sekiranya PAS benar-benar mahu memimpin Putrajaya, saya berpendapat mereka perlu mendengar pandangan pakar seperti beliau dan pakar-pakar dari kaum lain yang mempunyai kepakaran dalam percukaian dan kewangan awam. Persoalannya ialah: apakah model percukaian alternatif yang PAS mahu dan akan diperkenalkan?

Adakah PAS akan terus bergantung kepada sistem cukai sedia ada (SST dan GST) atau mempunyai keberanian untuk memperkenalkan pendekatan baharu yang lebih luas asasnya, lebih cekap kutipannya dan lebih adil kepada rakyat?

Jika EPT mampu direka dengan baik sehingga kutipan hasil kerajaan menjadi lebih cekap tanpa terlalu membebankan golongan berpendapatan rendah, ia boleh menjadi sebahagian daripada reset fiskal negara. Tetapi ini memerlukan kajian, kepakaran dan perancangan yang sangat teliti.

Kerajaan tetap memerlukan hasil yang mencukupi untuk membiayai kos pengurusan, belanjawan untuk pendidikan, kesihatan, keselamatan, pengangkutan awam, infrastruktur dan pembangunan negara. Justeru, PAS perlu menjelaskan bukan sahaja berapa banyak cukai yang mahu dikutip, tetapi daripada siapa, dengan cara bagaimana dan untuk membiayai apa.
Defisit, hutang dan ketirisan

Terkait dengan dasar fiskal ialah belanjawan defisit Malaysia setiap tahun yang telah melangkau lebih dua puluh lapan tahun, sejak 1998. Belanjawan defisit ini membuatkan hutang kerajaan terus meningkat, yang kini sudah melebihi RM1.38 trilion atau sejumlah 64% daripada kadar Keluaran Dalam Negara Kasar. Dalam keadaan sebegini, setiap ringgit wang negara dan wang rakyat sepatutnya diurus dengan penuh amanah, telus dan berdisiplin. Ini yang harus disahut oleh PAS.

Masalahnya bukan sekadar kerajaan berbelanja terlalu banyak. Persoalan yang lebih besar ialah ke mana wang itu dibelanjakan, berapa banyak yang benar-benar sampai kepada rakyat dan berapa banyak yang hilang akibat ketirisan, pembaziran, penyelewengan, rasuah dan salah guna kuasa.

Sebab itu, jika PAS benar-benar serius untuk mengambil alih Putrajaya, rakyat berhak menuntut satu kenyataan dan pendirian yang jelas, tegas dan tidak berkompromi mengenai rasuah dan salah guna kuasa, khususnya apabila ia melibatkan wang negara dan wang simpanan rakyat.

Tanpa kenyataan yang kukuh dan meyakinkan mengenai perkara ini, pendirian PAS boleh ditafsirkan sebagai tidak serius, lemah dan akhirnya memudaratkan negara. Apalagi di muktamar kali ini, PAS mengundang parti-parti politik yang terjebak dengan gejala rasuah dan salahguna kuasa tersebut.
Ini bukan lagi soal politik kepartian atau rakan kongsi politik. Ini soal wang negara dan wang rakyat, yang memerlukan kerangka polisi yang wajar dan kuat.

Apabila negara mempunyai hutang yang begitu besar dan terus berbelanja dalam keadaan belanjawan defisit, kerajaan tidak boleh pada masa yang sama membiarkan ruang untuk ketirisan, pembaziran dan penyelewengan terus terbuka dan berlaku.

Setiap ketirisan akhirnya perlu dibayar oleh rakyat -- sama ada melalui cukai yang lebih tinggi, pengurangan subsidi, pengurangan perkhidmatan awam, pinjaman baharu atau hutang yang akan ditanggung oleh generasi akan datang.
Oleh itu, PAS perlu menjelaskan dengan terang empat tunggak utama:

• Apakah langkah konkrit yang akan diambil untuk membanteras rasuah? • Apakah mekanisme yang akan digunapakai untuk menutup ruang ketirisan? • Apakah dasar baru yang akan diperkenalkan terhadap sistem perolehan kerajaan? • Apakah tindakan yang akan diambil terhadap mereka yang menyalahgunakan kuasa, termasuk jika mereka datang daripada parti atau gabungan politik sendiri?

Empat persoalan dan jawapan dari pihak PAS ini sangat penting. Rakyat tidak mahu mendengar janji membanteras rasuah hanya ketika PAS menjadi pembangkang. Rakyat mahu melihat apakah prinsip yang sama akan digunakan apabila PAS menjadi kerajaan dan berhadapan dengan pesalah dari orang dalam kalangan mereka sendiri atau rakan politik mereka. Yang salah, tetap salah, sama ada kawan atau lawan.

Berhubung gejala rasuah, kenyataan presiden PAS dimuktamar semalam tidak memberansangkan. Sila lihat 'Corruption in Malaysia weaponised to discredit rivals, claims Hadi'. Apakah kerajaan PAS kelak tidak akan menutup segala kebocoran dan ketirisan dalam sistem kewangan negara?
Jika kebocoran tidak ditutup, berapa banyak pun hasil yang dikutip, negara akan terus menghadapi masalah yang sama, tidak kira pesalahnya menganut agama apa sekalipun.

Ia bukan lagi isu moral semata-mata. Ia adalah isu ekonomi, isu kekuatan kewangan negara dan ianya juga, adalah isu masa depan generasi muda Malaysia. Sebab itu, isu gejala rasuah, ketirisan dan salah guna kuasa amat penting untuk dijadikan landasan sebenar polisi parti dan ia merangkumi sebahagian daripada dasar fiskal dan kewangan negara.
Jadi sebelum PAS meminta rakyat memberikan mandat untuk memimpin Putrajaya, mereka perlu terlebih dahulu menjawab satu soalan yang mudah tetapi sangat besar maknanya:
Apakah sebenarnya rancangan fiskal PAS untuk Malaysia?

3e8a758c7a64ac70: The US military's effort to prevent troops from being tracked by adversaries through purchased location data hasn't worked as well as anticipated, and lawmakers want to know why. US Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) and Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-NC) on Friday asked for an investigation by the Defense Department Inspector General into policies that have only partially stanched the flow of location data that allows military personnel to be tracked and targeted. In May, Wyden, Harrigan, and a bipartisan group of 12 other members of Congress released details about how commercially purchased location data – often captured by mobile apps and advertising SDKs – can be used to identify where US military personnel gather and to target those locations. They noted that the DoD has been aware of this threat since at least 2016. The lawmakers urged Defense Department CIO Kirsten A. Davies to take steps to mitigate this risk, including turning off advertising identifiers on DoD smartphones and issuing a policy requiring the disabling of advertising identifiers on all personal devices brought into DoD facilities or overseas. Since then, various military branches have blocked advertising identifiers on government-issued devices. According to the letter, "several DoD components – the Army, Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps, and Special Operations Command – confirm that they now disable advertising IDs on government-issued devices to protect their personnel from such threats." But that hasn't entirely eliminated the availability of location data tied to US military personnel. Citing ongoing reports, Wyden and Harrigan want to know why location data pinpointing the movement of troops continues to be available. "We commend these service branches for implementing this cybersecurity defensive best practice on government devices," they said in their letter [PDF] to the DoD IG. "However, recent reports regarding the continued availability of commercial location data originating from DoD facilities raise troubling questions." The two lawmakers speculate about the reason DoD policies have fallen short. One possibility, they say, is that some parts of the DoD turned off their advertising identifiers only as recently as July. Another, they say, is that disabling ad identifiers may no longer be sufficient to limit the availability of location data. And the third is that the location data is coming entirely from the personal devices of DoD personnel and contractors. Zach Edwards, staff threat researcher at Infoblox, told The Register in an email that it's good to hear all the military branches have disabled advertising IDs on their phones because it will make members of the military and their families safer, especially those serving in combat zones overseas. "This change will essentially ensure that military device location data isn't being included in bulk data sales being done by numerous vendors," he said. "It’s truly unfortunate that Google and Apple have not effectively reformed their mobile advertising IDs, even after it’s been well documented that it’s the primary piece of data being used by data brokers to connect up people’s mobile phone location data for bulk sales." Mobile advertising identifiers (MAIDs), Edwards explained, serve as join keys for tracking people – they can link different datasets. "So one core benefit is that military data won't be available for sale via data brokers, who will sell to literally anyone with a pulse and a credit card," said Edwards. "But the other slightly less obvious benefit is that this MAID was also being broadcast to all ad systems participating in the auctions." Edwards said that while states like California, Vermont, Texas, and Oregon have data broker registries, he's unaware of any Russian or Chinese ad tech vendors who have registered. And those companies, he said, partner with Western publishers and mobile apps to collect data anyway. "I think it's important to appreciate that these ad tech companies in Russia and China have also likely been getting MAID data from the programmatic ad tech auctions from members of the military, and companies in those countries have an obligation to share it with the state without any ability to appeal or provide any external notice," he said. ®

dbcf89bb6cac86e8: After nearly eight years, ESA and JAXA's BepiColombo spacecraft is finally nearing Mercury, as engineers begin the arrival sequence by jettisoning the power module that got it this far. The spacecraft stack separated from the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) on September 3 at around 1400 CEST. After a tense few minutes, controllers confirmed that a preliminary Doppler signal had been detected, indicating that the MTM had separated successfully; by 1552 CEST, it was confirmed that signals had been picked up, indicating that all had gone to plan. The solar panels of the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) were charging the spacecraft's batteries. The next stage involves dropping into orbit around Mercury on November 21. Then the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO) – aka Mio – will be released between December 9 and 10, and a week later MPO will start moving to its final orbit over 480 x 1500 km, with science commencing in April 2027. The arrival is a year later than planned. BepiColombo was supposed to have been orbiting Mercury in December 2025, but problems with the spacecraft's Solar Electric Power (SEP) system meant the trajectory had to be rethought, which extended the spacecraft's cruise. BepiColombo is no stranger to Mercury and has performed six flybys of the planet since 2021. It has also conducted flybys of Venus and Earth following its 2018 launch. The spacecraft is an impressive example of international cooperation. The MPO and MTM are ESA contributions, while the MMO comes from JAXA. ESA also provided the sunshield to protect the MMO during transit. This sunshield will be ejected after the MMO is released. The MPO is the big brother of the BepiColombo partnership, with a main body measuring 2.4 x 2.2 x 1.7 m and a mass of 1,230 kg (including an 85 kg science payload). JAXA's MMO is 1.8 m in diameter and 1.1 m high, and weighs 255 kg (45 kg of which is the science payload). While MPO is 3-axis stabilized and nadir-pointing, MMO will be spin-stabilized at 15 rpm, with its spin axis 90 degrees to the Sun. The goal of the mission is a study of Mercury, "from the structure and dynamics of its magnetosphere and how it interacts with the solar wind, to the properties of its large iron core and the origin of its magnetic field." The initial mission at Mercury is planned for one Earth year (approximately four Mercury years), although it could be extended by another Earth year. ®

eb565a991b544039: From the Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah
For most of my life, I have described myself, rather cheerfully, as a Jill of all trades and master of none.
I have tried my hand at almost everything.

I cook. I sew. I embroider. I design. I garden. I collect. I write. I make things. I take things apart and put them together again. I become fascinated by something, pursue it with enormous enthusiasm, and before long, another curiosity comes knocking at the door.
My hands have never been very good at keeping still, and neither, I suspect, has my mind.
But there was always one thing I never really thought of myself as being.
A scholar.
That belonged to another world: to academics, professors, historians and people who seemed to have known from a very young age exactly what they wanted to study and what they wanted to become.
I was already 64 when I returned seriously to academic life.
At an age when one is perhaps expected to slow down, I did precisely the opposite.
I went back to school.
And somewhere between lectures, books, manuscripts, footnotes and many very late nights, something quite unexpected happened.
I fell in love with learning.
Not with examinations. Not with grades. Not even with the idea of obtaining a degree.
I fell in love with the chase.

One question led to another. One footnote opened another door. A sentence written hundreds of years ago could keep me awake at night. I began looking at old manuscripts and wondering who had held them, who had written them, why certain words had been chosen, and what they might tell us that history had forgotten.
Then I met the Hukum Kanun Pahang.
Or perhaps, more accurately, I met it again.
It had been there all along. But for the first time, I began to see it not merely as an old manuscript belonging to Pahang, but as a voice from another age.
And I began asking questions.
Too many questions, according to some people around me.

One discovery became another. Melaka led me to Pahang. Pahang led me to Sultan Abdul Ghaffar Muhyiddin Shah. The laws led me to the sea. The sea led me to sovereignty. And somewhere along the way, the thesis I thought I was going to write began refusing to become the thesis I had planned.
That was perhaps my first real lesson as a student.
Do not tell history what you want it to say.
Listen to what the evidence is trying to tell you.
So I followed it.

I followed it through manuscripts and histories, through laws and royal genealogies, through ports and rivers, through Melaka and Pahang, sometimes with excitement, sometimes with frustration, and occasionally with tears.
And on July 27, at the age of 65, I submitted my Master’s thesis:
The Hukum Kanun Pahang: A Sovereign Malay-Islamic Constitution.
A few weeks later, I received my examination results.
The average mark from the two examiners was 91%.
My internal examiner recommended the thesis for acceptance without any modifications or amendments in content, while my external examiner required only very minor corrections.
I read the reports.
And then I cried.
I cried, and I screamed.
Not very scholarly behaviour, perhaps, but after months of work, doubt, discovery, late nights and wondering whether I had understood the manuscript correctly, I could not help myself.
I had never expected this.
But it was not only the marks, or even the absence of corrections from one examiner and the very minor corrections from the other, that moved me.
Both examiners believed that the work should go beyond the examination room.

My internal examiner wrote that the thesis demonstrated “originality, coherence, and scholarly adequacy” and was therefore “suitable for publication.” Its strength, he observed, lay in reframing the Hukum Kanun Pahang as a sovereign Malay-Islamic constitution, embedding Sharīʿah principles within adat, and highlighting the balance between royal authority and accountability.
He concluded that these contributions provided “a fresh civilisational lens that enriches Malay legal historiography.”

My external examiner similarly recommended that the findings of the thesis should be disseminated through academic publications and conference presentations, to highlight their importance to Malaysia’s inherited constitutional and legal identity.
Those words meant a great deal to me.

I had begun this journey simply wanting to understand an old manuscript that had captured my imagination. I never imagined that at the end of it, my examiners would tell me that what I had discovered deserved to travel beyond my thesis and into the wider academic world.
And then I laughed.
Because after spending most of my life calling myself a Jill of all trades and master of none, at 66 years old I had finally managed to become—
a Master of one.
But perhaps that is not really what this story is about.
It is not about 91%.
It is not even about a Master’s degree.
It is about discovering, rather late in life, that curiosity has no retirement age.

We are very fond of putting ages upon things. There is an age to study, an age to marry, an age to raise children, an age to build a career and, apparently, an age when we should begin quietly withdrawing from new adventures.
I am beginning to think that is nonsense.
Some flowers bloom in spring.
Others take their time.

Perhaps being a late bloomer does not mean that one has arrived late. Perhaps all those earlier years, the cooking, sewing, creating, reading, raising children, serving, listening, observing, succeeding, failing, beginning again, were not detours at all.
Perhaps they were preparation.
Because when I finally entered that library and opened those manuscripts, I did not arrive there only as a student.
I brought a lifetime with me.
And perhaps that was my advantage.
I had spent 66 years learning before I realised that I was a learner.
I had spent a lifetime searching before I discovered what I was searching for.
I had spent years calling myself a Jill of all trades and master of none.
Then, very late in the garden, a little flower appeared.
And I discovered that I had been growing all along.
I am a late bloomer.
And I think I rather like blooming late.
But above all, I know that all knowledge comes from Allah. Whatever I have learned, whatever I have discovered, and whatever little contribution I may have made are only by His permission and grace.
Alhamdulillah.

I thank Allah for giving me the opportunity, the strength and the curiosity to continue learning at this stage of my life. I pray that whatever knowledge He has entrusted to me may be used well, shared generously and become something of benefit to others.
I have just registered for my PhD.
And somewhere in the fifteenth century, Parameswara is waiting for me.

P/S: My husband insists that I clarify one important point: I met him before I met Hukum Kanun Pahang. So, in the interests of historical accuracy, let the record show that he was my first great discovery.

The Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah, holds a master’s degree from the International Institute of Islamic Thought and Civilisation (ISTAC), International Islamic University Malaysia.
8abf3bff1da3daba: Mujurlah Presiden Umno Zahid Hamidi tidak hadir pada majlis perasmian muktamar PAS semalam. Saya kata 'mujur' kerana jika beliau hadir beliau akan dengar ucapan dasar Presiden PAS Hadi Awang secara langsung. Loud and clear.

Mungkin Zahid akan merasa 'disakiti'. Jika tidak sakit hati mungkin terkejut dan terperanjat kerana apa yang dilaungkan Hadi itu dilakukan ketika PAS sedang ghairah mahu jalin kerjasama dengan Umno, berlatarkan electoral pact yang berjaya di Johor dan Negeri Sembilan tempoh hari.

Mungkinkah Zahid sudah menghidu atau dapat info apa yang akan diucapkan Hadi? Wallahualam. Apa pun Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki si setiausaha agung Umno hadir mewakili Zahid. Tak tahulah saya sama ada berdesing telinga beliau mendengar ucapan Hadi.

At least this part of the Hadi speech: "Setiap kerusi Dewan Undangan Negeri dan Parlimen yang telah dimenangi pada PRU 15 wajib dipertahankan". Perhatikan istilah yang Hadi gunakan yakni 'wajib'. Kata Hadi lagi: "Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah dan Perlis (SG4) sebagai 'negeri pangkalan' mesti terus dikekalkan penguasaannya, diperkukuh pentadbiran serta dilaksana agenda Islam mengikut bidang kuasa negeri."
That does not leave much for Umno-BN jika kerjasama dengan PAS dijalin. Sebenarnya sehari sebelum ucapan Hadi, mood 'PAS menguasai semua' sudah dirasai pada muktamar Pemuda PAS.

Umpamanya Ketua Pemuda PAS Kedah Ilyas Ahmad dipetik berkata usaha menyatukan umat Islam di peringkat persekutuan perlu dipimpin oleh PAS dan PAS juga tidak seharusnya lagi memberi laluan calon perdana menteri kepada parti lain. That is as clear as it can get. Beberapa perwakilan muktamar juga bercakap apa yang PAS mesti buat jika menang PRU16.

Kata Ketua Penyelidik Ilham Centre Yusri Ibrahim menerusi catatan di Facebook, penegasan PAS akan membuka episod baru dalam kebarangkalian kerjasama Umno-PAS menuju PRU16. Beliau ambil Terengganu sebagai contoh, "Jika PAS bertegas, hanya ada satu kerusi Parlimen dan lima kerusi DUN berbaki untuk ditandingi oleh Umno jika kerjasama dimeterai. Tetapi semua kerusi tersebut disandang oleh Bersatu."
Maka kata Yusri, "sudah tentu Wawasan akan bermatian menuntut dan mempertahankan kerusi tersebut kerana kepada Wawasan merekalah pewaris pusaka Bersatu dalam Perikatan Nasional."
"Jika kerusi tersebut dibahagi sama rata, Umno Terengganu berpotensi bertanding sekitar tiga kerusi sahaja dalam PRU16 nanti. Inilah scenario awal yang boleh difahami."
Itu belum lagi kita bercakap mengenai kerusi Parlimen dan DUN negeri-negeri lain.

Dalam pada itu, penganalisis James Chin dari Universiti Tasmania semalam dipetik FMT berkata Umno tampak cuba melemahkan perdana menteri meskipun berikrar menyokong Anwar Ibrahim sehingga tamat penggal Parlimen.

"Mereka mengenakan tekanan kerana tidak mahu hilang momentum (setelah menang PRN Johor dan Negeri Sembilan bersama PN serta confident menang PRN Melaka kelak). Adakah Anwar akan tunduk? Saya rasa masih awal untuk bercakap mengenainya. Anwar juga sedang mengatur perikatan baharu tanpa Umno," kata Chin.
Chin menjangkakan hubungan PH-BN akan semakin buruk sambil Umno terus berdolak dalik. Saya setuju dan tidak mungkin Anwar dan PH tidak perasan.

Berikutan ucapan Hadi semalam, Umno tertekan. Jika usul wajib berkait kerjasama dengan Umno diterima sebelum muktamar ditangguhkan hari ini, Umno tertekan juga tetapi saya tidak pasti adakah ia relevan memandangkan apa yang diucapkan Hadi yang saya sebut tadi.

Amat menarik apa agaknya reaksi Perhimpunan Agung Umno terhadap perkembangan di muktamar PAS. PAU akan berlangsung minggu depan yakni 9 hingga 12 September. Menarik juga kerana kepimpinan tertinggi PAS diundang ke upacara perasmian. Adakah Hadi akan hadir? Iya, kata Asyraf.

Menutup penulisan ini saya ulang apa yang pernah dinyatakan pada artikel terdahulu iaitu Umno sedang buat apa yang ia tuduh PAS buat dulu sehingga terkuburnya Muafakat Nasional. Apa yang PAS buat waktu itu? Bermain dua kolam, kata Umno. PAS berbaik dengan Umno dan pada masa sama berbaik-baik dengan Bersatu, musuh ketat Umno.
Sekarang Umno berbaik-baik dengan PH di peringkat persekutuan dan berbaik-baik dengan PAS di peringkat negeri sambil menyerang PH. Ertinya Umno main dua kolam.
Bagi saya sudah sudahlah main dua kolam. You can't have your cake and eat it too. Itu kata omputih. Orang Melayu kata simple je: "jangan nak makan kelilinglah".
